overview.purpose: To examine what the quantitative evidence shows about whether the ability to understand and apply health information translates into the actions adults take to maintain or improve their health.
overview.title: The Relationship Between Health Literacy and Health-Related Behaviors Among Adults: A Review of Quantitative Research

i04.text: Association is not causation. Cross-sectional studies show relationships but cannot show health literacy caused a behavior.

i01.text: Core question: does the ability to understand and apply health information translate into the actions people take to maintain or improve their health?

i07.text: Financial resources, access, culture, motivation, social support and competing responsibilities may shape whether people act on information.

i03.text: Knowing what to do is not the same as doing it. Strongest articles measure both health literacy and at least one behavior.

i09.gapType: Practical applications for Health Is Lit
i09.text: Health Is Lit: implementation moves at the speed of trust and education. Findings could inform practical education resources.

i05.text: Health outcomes (blood pressure, hospitalization) are not the same as behaviors. Keep outcome-only studies out of the core 25.

i08.text: International studies: account for differences in health systems, health education, socioeconomic conditions and access to care.

i06.text: Example: someone knows their LDL is high and understands the risk. Do they change diet, exercise, take medication, attend follow-up?

i10.text: Watch for whether studies use validated health literacy and behavior instruments. Measurement differences may explain inconsistent findings.

i02.text: Health literacy is not the same as health knowledge. It includes accessing, understanding, evaluating and applying information.

a01.text: Met with Dr. Rae about research direction. Date to add.

q08.text: Do intervention studies need to measure health literacy itself, or is evaluating a health literacy-based intervention enough?

a04.text: Chapter 2 focuses on research published from 2021 to present. Historical and seminal references may be used in Chapter 1.

a05.text: Do not develop a research question that needs more variables or evidence than the literature can support.

a02.text: Narrow the topic to avoid too many variables. Focus on the relationship or effect of health literacy on patient health behaviors.

q03.text: Confirm the preliminary inclusion and exclusion criteria before treating them as final.

q04.text: Confirm there are no geographic restrictions, so international studies can be included.

q07.text: Are single-item health literacy screeners acceptable as a measure?

a07.text: Laboratory values stay a relevant example of clinical health information, not a required component of every study.

q06.text: Should samples that include 15 to 17 year olds be excluded, or accepted if most participants are adults?

q01.text: Do cross-sectional studies count as qualifying quantitative research, or does she want a minimum number of RCTs or longitudinal studies? (31 of 36 verified studies are cross-sectional.)

a03.text: Find at least 25 relevant quantitative primary research articles. Systematic reviews, meta-analyses and qualitative-only studies do not count toward the 25.

a08.text: Simplified the focus to the relationship between health literacy and health-related behaviors, after the advisor meeting.

a06.text: Conduct a more thorough literature search, prepare a research synthesis, and send the refined RQs and synthesis to Dr. Rae. After her review, move forward with the topic approval package to Dr. Easterbrooks.

q02.text: Is one primary question with one subquestion (RQ1 and RQ1a) acceptable?

a09.text: Literature search recommendation (not yet decided): keep RQ1 as the primary question and use the alternative RQ2 as a focused subquestion (RQ1a). Drop the original RQ2 wording, since "how" and "influence" imply causation and 31 of 36 studies are cross-sectional. Keep conclusions about which behaviors are strongest descriptive, not a pooled effect size. Working title still fits.
